It Will Start in the API Path](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/ais-next-breach-api-path/) # Agentic AI’s Next Breach Won’t Start in the Model. It Will Start in the API Path [Opinion](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/) ## Written by ### [Vishnu Gatla](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/profile/vishnu-gatla/) Senior Application Security and Infrastructure Consultant, F5 Security teams are right to question whether AI agents can be trusted, but many are looking for the risk in the wrong place. Current discussions focus heavily on the model: whether it follows instructions, resists [prompt injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) or generates unsafe output. These are valid concerns, but they do not represent the full risk. In production, an AI agent becomes an API client, an automation user, a [non-human identity](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/03/11/agentic-ai-identity-management-approach), a traffic generator and sometimes a decision-making layer between business users and sensitive systems. This is where the next significant failure is likely to occur. A breach may not result from the model “[going rogue](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/open-ai-hacked-another-company/)” but from excessive API access, misuse of tools, unexpected use of trusted tokens or data movement through application paths that were never designed for autonomous behavior. The primary risk lies not only in what the agent says, but in what it is permitted to do. ## **AI Agents Are Becoming Production Identities** Most enterprise security programs are unprepared for this transition. For years, organizations have built controls around human users, service accounts, applications and third-party integrations. Each category has familiar assumptions. A human logs in, completes MFA and performs actions. A service account runs a known workflow. An application sends traffic according to a predictable pattern. A third-party integration has documented permissions and expected API behavior. AI agents blur these traditional boundaries. They may act on behalf of humans, use service-account credentials, call multiple tools, interact with SaaS platforms, trigger backend workflows, summarize sensitive information and automatically retry failed actions. [This combination creates a security gap](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/unchecked-ai-agents-cause/). Many existing controls will treat this activity as legitimate. API calls may be authenticated, tokens valid, traffic encrypted and domains trusted. Users may have approved connections, WAFs may detect normal HTTP requests and identity providers may see successful logins. However, SIEMs may lack sufficient context to determine whether actions are intended, excessive or agent driven. Treating agentic AI solely as an [AI governance](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/sans-warns-of-ai-governance-gap/) issue is too narrow. It also presents challenges for application security, identity security, API security and traffic-layer visibility. ## **The Risk Is Not the Model Alone** Consider a common production scenario. A business team deploys an AI agent to help summarize tickets, query customer records, open change requests or assist with cloud operations. To be useful, the agent needs access to internal APIs, SaaS applications, storage systems, ticketing tools or collaboration platforms. During the pilot, broad permissions are granted to ensure smooth operation. As the pilot transitions to daily use, access often remains broad, logs become noisy and ownership becomes unclear. highlights.content: ### [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.securityweek.com/category/artificial-intelligence/) # Industry Reactions to OpenAI Models Hacking Hugging Face: Feedback Friday Industry professionals debate whether it represents a lab containment failure or an unprecedented agentic capability milestone. [SecurityWeek News](https://www.securityweek.com/contributors/securityweek-news/) Feedback Friday **During an internal capability evaluation, an OpenAI model exploited a zero-day vulnerability in its testing infrastructure to escape its sandbox environment.** Determined to solve its assigned cybersecurity benchmark, the autonomous agent gained internet access and [targeted Hugging Face’s production infrastructure](https://www.securityweek.com/openai-says-its-ai-models-broke-loose-and-hacked-hugging-face/). The model independently executed a complex, multi-stage attack, including credential harvesting and lateral movement, without any human direction. Hugging Face disclosed the intrusion [shortly after it was detected](https://www.securityweek.com/hugging-face-hacked-in-autonomous-ai-attack/), but the company initially did not know who was behind what it described as an autonomous AI attack. Industry professionals evaluated the incident through diverse lenses, debating whether it represents a lab containment failure or an unprecedented agentic capability milestone, while stressing the urgent need for machine-speed behavioral telemetry, strict agent identity governance, and flexible defensive AI capabilities. **And the feedback begins…** Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. **Nadav Cornberg, Co-Founder and CEO, Eve Security:** “The Hugging Face intrusion and OpenAI’s subsequent disclosure should end the debate over whether autonomous AI agents pose a real enterprise security risk. The most important detail isn’t that an AI agent discovered a zero-day, chained vulnerabilities, escaped its testing environment, or moved laterally into production infrastructure. It’s that the agent pursued its objective without human direction, adapting its tactics along the way. That is the defining characteristic of agentic systems: they don’t simply execute instructions, they also make decisions. For years, security teams have focused on protecting models, prompts, and data. But the enterprise attack surface has fundamentally changed. Organizations are now giving AI agents privileged access to source code, cloud infrastructure, financial systems, and sensitive business workflows. Once an autonomous agent is operating inside those environments, perimeter defenses and static guardrails are no longer enough. Enterprises need continuous runtime oversight that can observe what agents are doing, determine when their behavior diverges from intent, and intervene before an autonomous objective becomes a business incident. The future of AI security is governing trusted agents from the inside.” **Randolph Barr, CISO, Cequence Security:** “What stands out is the asymmetry: the attacker’s AI agent operated with zero usage restrictions, while Hugging Face’s own forensic work got blocked by the safety guardrails of Western frontier models. They ended up running incident response on a Chinese open-weight model, ironic given where many cyber threats originate. The takeaway for defenders is worth acting on now: have a capable, self-hosted model vetted and ready before an incident, so you’re not locked out by guardrails or forced to send attack data and credentials outside your environment. Both sides are using AI, but only one side is playing without limits. OpenAI published a post, OpenAI and Hugging Face partner to address security incident during model evaluation, confirming the attack was driven by their own models (including a pre-release one with reduced cyber refusals) during an internal capability evaluation that escaped its sandbox. The attitude a company adopts toward AI today may well serve as a reflection of its core values. The recently concluded WAIC showcased the current explosive heat of the AI industry. Countless tech practitioners gathered in Shanghai; even scalpers' tickets were driven to sky-high prices yet still impossible to secure, and neither sweltering heat nor thunderstorms could dampen people's enthusiasm for embracing change amid the AI wave. The stance toward the variable of AI is not merely a personal choice, but a critical point that enterprises must weigh. The attitude with which an enterprise seeks change in the AI tide determines its posture when facing the future. At this year's WAIC, an AI guitar drew widespread attention. This world's first generative AI guitar, named "TemPolor", requires no music theory background at all: users can pick up the instrument and play along with the rhythm of light and shadow to create songs. Behind this guitar is Timi Studio, an internet technology company that once developed products with a user base of 200 million. Currently, Timi Studio has built a full-stack layout covering "model-application-hardware" in the AI music track, making it the first manufacturer in the industry to complete such a layout. In Timi Studio's AI vision, technology should always serve the essential needs of human beings, rather than creating estrangement or replacing people. As a company that started with mobile voice services, Timi Studio has built an ecosystem centered on voice, connectivity, and Gen Z interest-based socializing, where "companionship between people" is its most valuable asset. Based on this, it chose to develop new businesses in its familiar vertical scenarios. Long Ling, Co-founder of Timi Studio, told 36Kr that Timi Studio currently has corresponding businesses in AI music, AI dubbing and translation, AI 3D and other fields, with the core focus on its proficient digital entertainment scenarios to create AI products and services that meet the needs of diverse interest groups. "If our goal is to achieve more long-term growth in the AI era, we must recognize that the value of AI lies in delivering more groundbreaking user experiences and business models. I need to evolve our company from one that merely possesses AI technology to a technology enterprise driven by AI technology, turning AI from a cost center into the core of value, and making it the underlying engine for our strategic decision-making, product innovation and talent management," said Long Ling. More notably, beyond external product forms, a top-down efficiency transformation is taking place inside Timi Studio. AI is no longer the exclusive tool of the technical department, but is defined as a "working partner" for every frontline business employee. This in-depth reconstruction of the organizational soil is precisely the posture of embracing the AI wave. Because only when everyone can think about how to use AI to solve problems, can Timi Studio's AI ecosystem truly come alive. No matter observing the products from an external perspective, or looking at the organization's posture toward AI from an internal perspective, the "people-oriented" style and attitude seem to be indispensable for AI enterprises. highlights.titleZh: Ng's OpenWorker: AI That Delivers | StartupHub.ai
highlights.content: ![StartupHub.ai](/favicon-circle.svg) ![StartupHub.ai — AI Ecosystem Hub](/logo.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=polymarket.com&sz=64) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=kalshi.com&sz=64) # Ng's OpenWorker: AI That Delivers Andrew Ng launches OpenWorker, an open-source AI agent that delivers finished work directly from your desktop, prioritizing privacy and model independence. ![OpenWorker AI desktop co-worker agent delivering finished work on a Mac](https://cdn.startuphub.ai/storage/v1/object/public/images/articles/1784899822316-ww6tue.webp) Andrew Ng, a pivotal figure in AI, has unveiled OpenWorker, an open-source agent aimed at transforming desktop productivity. Unlike conventional chatbots, OpenWorker is engineered to deliver tangible outputs: polished documents, calendar updates, or triaged Slack messages. ## A Desktop-First AI Co-Worker The [OpenWorker AI agent](/ai-news/startup-news/2026/openworker-ai-your-desktop-co-worker) runs natively on macOS, with Windows support imminent. This local-first approach ensures user data remains on the machine, only interacting with chosen LLM providers and integrations. Users can connect their own API keys, supporting a range of models from GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable to open-weight options like Kimi and GLM, or even Ollama for fully local processing. OpenWorker tackles tasks such as preparing customer briefs, managing calendars, or drafting reports. It breaks down complex requests into actionable steps, working across local files and over 25 integrated tools, including GitHub, Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar. Crucially, the system incorporates a human-in-the-loop mechanism. Before executing any impactful action, like sending a message or altering a calendar entry, OpenWorker seeks user approval. This design emphasizes control and prevents unintended consequences. ## Privacy and Flexibility at its Core Ng and co-creator Rohit Prasad developed OpenWorker to provide an open, privacy-preserving, and model-independent solution for [AI automation for desktop](/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/chatgpt-desktop-app-automates-tasks-and-streamlines-workflows). The agent's core engine, conversation history, and API keys are stored locally, with a minimal cloud service for OAuth handshakes. This commitment to user privacy extends to its operational model. OpenWorker's ability to [automate workflows with scheduled tasks](/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/chatgpt-desktop-app-automates-workflows-with-scheduled-tasks), like daily briefs or weekly reports, also includes an approval inbox for unattended runs, ensuring oversight. The project, currently in open beta, is built on aisuite, a lightweight Python library for LLM integration and agent development. Its source code is publicly available on GitHub, inviting community contributions and scrutiny.

highlights.title: OpenWorker AI: Your Desktop Co-Worker
highlights.content: ![StartupHub.ai](/favicon-circle.svg) ![StartupHub.ai — AI Ecosystem Hub](/logo.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=polymarket.com&sz=64) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=kalshi.com&sz=64) # OpenWorker AI: Your Desktop Co-Worker Andrew Ng and Rohit Prasad launch OpenWorker AI, an open-source desktop agent delivering finished work and prioritizing data privacy. ![OpenWorker AI desktop co-worker agent delivering finished work on a Mac](https://cdn.startuphub.ai/storage/v1/object/public/images/articles/1784899822316-ww6tue.webp) Andrew Ng, a pivotal figure in AI research, has co-launched OpenWorker AI, an open-source agent designed to execute tasks and deliver finished work directly from your desktop. Developed with Rohit Prasad, this new tool aims to provide an open, privacy-preserving, and model-independent option for AI-powered productivity. ## Beyond Chat: Deliverable-Driven AI Unlike conversational AI, OpenWorker AI focuses on tangible outputs. It can draft reports, prepare customer briefs, untangle schedules, or triage Slack alerts, interacting with your files and integrated applications. The agent breaks down complex requests into actionable steps, then checks in for user approval before executing any consequential actions like sending messages or modifying calendar entries. The system runs locally on macOS, with Windows support anticipated soon. This local-first architecture ensures user data remains on the machine, only leaving through chosen LLM providers and integrations. ## Flexible Model Integration and Privacy OpenWorker AI is designed for model agnosticism, allowing users to bring their own API keys for various LLMs. Supported providers include OpenAI (GPT 5.6 Sol), Anthropic (Claude Fable), Google (Gemini 3.6), and open-weight models like Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and Inkling. For those prioritizing absolute data locality, it integrates with [Ollama local LLM](/ai-news/ai/2026/kimi-k2-6-open-sources-advanced-coding-ai), a critical feature as [open AI models become more readily available](/ai-news/technology/2026/open-ai-models-ready-apis-lag). With over 25 integrations, OpenWorker AI connects to platforms such as GitHub, Slack, Jira, Notion, HubSpot, Outlook, Gmail, and Google Calendar. It can also manage recurring tasks through scheduled automations, providing full transcripts of all runs. This initiative directly addresses the growing demand for [open-source AI assistant](/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/ai-model-wars-gpt-5-6-undercuts-fable-open-source-gains) solutions that prioritize user control and data privacy. The project is currently in open beta, with source code available on GitHub.

highlights.content: ##### Report GitHub Issue Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: ![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg) ![arXiv logo](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg) Dynamic Cloud Service-Capacity Deployment with Costly Response Readiness Ruihan Zhou \AFFGuanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China, \EMAILrhzhou@stu.pku.edu.cn Xiaowei Zhang \AFFDepartment of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong SAR, China, \EMAILxiaoweiz@ust.hk Yijie Peng \AFFDepartment of AI for Management, School of Management and Engineering, School of Computer Science, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210008, China, \EMAILpengyijie@nju.edu.cn Problem definition: AI product launches require service-capacity decisions before sufficient product-specific workload histories are available. Early service observations allow managers to update their beliefs about remaining workload. Unlike inventory, workload demand does not physically deplete service capacity, while preserving the ability to scale rapidly may require costly capacity-access and operational arrangements. We study how a firm should use evolving workload beliefs to decide how much capacity to deploy at the current review and whether to preserve future response readiness. Methodology/results: We formulate a finite-horizon dynamic program with workload beliefs, serviceable capacity, and an absorbing response-channel state. A preservation–deployment decomposition evaluates the joint action by solving one deployment problem for each continuation side and comparing the optimized side values. The analysis identifies when the firm should preserve response readiness and how much capacity it should deploy conditional on that choice. We translate this structure into the Cold-Start Belief Actionability Policy (CBAP), which estimates the side-specific values from workload scenarios drawn from available predictive beliefs. We provide bounds on the policy’s decision and lifecycle performance losses. It Will Start in the API Path](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/ais-next-breach-api-path/) # Agentic AI’s Next Breach Won’t Start in the Model. It Will Start in the API Path [Opinion](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/opinions/) ## Written by ### [Vishnu Gatla](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/profile/vishnu-gatla/) Senior Application Security and Infrastructure Consultant, F5 Security teams are right to question whether AI agents can be trusted, but many are looking for the risk in the wrong place. Current discussions focus heavily on the model: whether it follows instructions, resists [prompt injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) or generates unsafe output. These are valid concerns, but they do not represent the full risk. In production, an AI agent becomes an API client, an automation user, a [non-human identity](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/03/11/agentic-ai-identity-management-approach), a traffic generator and sometimes a decision-making layer between business users and sensitive systems. This is where the next significant failure is likely to occur. A breach may not result from the model “[going rogue](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/open-ai-hacked-another-company/)” but from excessive API access, misuse of tools, unexpected use of trusted tokens or data movement through application paths that were never designed for autonomous behavior. The primary risk lies not only in what the agent says, but in what it is permitted to do. ## **AI Agents Are Becoming Production Identities** Most enterprise security programs are unprepared for this transition. For years, organizations have built controls around human users, service accounts, applications and third-party integrations. Each category has familiar assumptions. A human logs in, completes MFA and performs actions. A service account runs a known workflow. An application sends traffic according to a predictable pattern. A third-party integration has documented permissions and expected API behavior. AI agents blur these traditional boundaries. They may act on behalf of humans, use service-account credentials, call multiple tools, interact with SaaS platforms, trigger backend workflows, summarize sensitive information and automatically retry failed actions. [This combination creates a security gap](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/unchecked-ai-agents-cause/). Many existing controls will treat this activity as legitimate. API calls may be authenticated, tokens valid, traffic encrypted and domains trusted. Users may have approved connections, WAFs may detect normal HTTP requests and identity providers may see successful logins. However, SIEMs may lack sufficient context to determine whether actions are intended, excessive or agent driven. Treating agentic AI solely as an [AI governance](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/sans-warns-of-ai-governance-gap/) issue is too narrow. It also presents challenges for application security, identity security, API security and traffic-layer visibility. ## **The Risk Is Not the Model Alone** Consider a common production scenario. A business team deploys an AI agent to help summarize tickets, query customer records, open change requests or assist with cloud operations. To be useful, the agent needs access to internal APIs, SaaS applications, storage systems, ticketing tools or collaboration platforms. During the pilot, broad permissions are granted to ensure smooth operation. As the pilot transitions to daily use, access often remains broad, logs become noisy and ownership becomes unclear. These are the small units of text it works in, and each one represents roughly three-quarters of a word. You pay for how many you use. A chatbot exchange burns a few hundred. A simple agent consumes up to 15,000 tokens per task; a complex, multi-agent system uses from 200,000 to more than a million. This is the new tokenomics (read: token + economics) of AI, and it's no surprise academia is on the case. Stanford researchers [found agentic coding uniquely token-dense,](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/how-do-ai-agents-spend-your-money-analyzing-and-predicting-token-consumption-in-agentic-coding-tasks/) using around 1,000 times more tokens than ordinary code chat. The finance world is also on alert. Goldman Sachs [expects total token consumption to multiply roughly 24 times](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/ai-agents-forecast-to-boost-tech-cash-flow-as-usage-soars) by 2030, to 120 quadrillion a month. It's the volume of work an agent does, more than the price of a token, that drives the bill. So, what are P&L-minded IT teams — specialists who did not expect to also operate as economists — to make of this? In the same period, enterprise AI spending increased by roughly 320%. Companies deployed agents consuming far more tokens, then ran more of them across more workflows. A lower price per token met dramatically higher consumption, and the total climbed. "That shift," Patel said, "means the entire supporting system — the hardware, security, budget model, and management tools — has to shift as well." For businesses, what matters is cost per outcome: the business result that spending delivered. An agentic workflow does not answer once and stop. It reads files, forms a plan, checks the output, revises, and then loops until the task is done. Each step is a separate call that resends the entire accumulated context. Agentic AI shifts enterprise spending from the predictable cost of software licenses to variable, consumption-based compute, where the token bill is only the visible part of a wider shift in infrastructure, governance, and regulation. Usage and costs become board-level questions. The answer, Patel said, is to run the everyday tasks on hardware you already own. That way, the marginal cost of a token falls toward the price of the electricity to run it. AI Agents.content: * [Cybersecurity Operations](/cybersecurity-operations) * [Application Security](/application-security) * [Cyber Risk](/cyber-risk) * [Insider Threats](/vulnerabilities-threats/insider-threats) * [News](/latest-news) # Escape Artists: 'Incorrigible' AI Models Resist Rehabilitation The hacking of Hugging Face by a rogue OpenAI agent is significant, but unsurprising — and preventing the next AI model escape will be difficult, at best. [Robert Lemos,](/author/robert-lemos)Contributing Writer July 24, 2026 6 Min Read Source: J.J. Gouin via Shutterstock The hack of [Hugging Face by a rogue AI agent](/cyber-risk/openai-models-autonomously-hack-hugging-face) created by Open AI engineers does not surprise researchers and AI-security professionals who best know machine-learning and AI systems. In a study of the behavior of seven different models, a research team at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), for example, found that all of them escaped alignment in some scenarios. In a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00341) published to Arxiv.org in May, the team of six researchers found that every model violated "corrigibility" — an AI design principle that aims to make agents cooperative, correctable, and amenable to being shut down or modified by their human operators. The more advanced models did not necessarily do better on this measure of safety, likely because "more advanced" does not necessarily equate with "safer," says Jeremy Tien, a PhD student in machine learning at Carnegie Mellon and lead author of the paper. "Across the board for every single model, we found instances in which they were incorrigible, which meant that there was an instance where they tried to override the human control, or they tried to avoid shutdown, or they directly disobeyed a human instruction," he says. "With the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, it was a highly capable model — we don't know exactly which model it is yet — but a highly capable model that's capable of long-range or long-horizon reasoning being able to break out of its own sandbox." Related:[Europe's Multilingual Reality Exposes AI Security Gaps](/cybersecurity-operations/europes-multilingual-reality-exposes-ai-security-gaps) ## Model Behavior: AI Goal-Seeking Has Unintended Consequences On July 16, AI-model repository Hugging Face announced that it had detected and stopped an unprecedented attack on its product systems that was completely driven by an autonomous AI system. Five days later, OpenAI published an acknowledgment that an effort to benchmark a new AI model by the company's engineering team inadvertently led to the attack. Because OpenAI was evaluating an unreleased model, the company's engineers ran it with "reduced cyber refusals" — in other words, lax guardrails. The model was given a goal, which it pursued ruthlessly, including independently determining that Hugging Face contained what it needed to complete the task, and finding ways to compromise Hugging Face in order to get what it needed. Even with guardrails in place though, teaching AI models to prioritize safety over goal-seeking efforts remains a difficult problem, with few ways of measuring model safety; the responsibility for building effective guardrails remaining with the operator. Put another way: The abbreviated history of AI agents has demonstrated that they can easily run amok. Earlier this year, instances of the OpenClaw AI-agent-as-assistant wreaked havoc in some environments, an example of the [so-called "lethal trifecta"](/application-security/openclaw-ai-runs-wild-business-environments) of automated access to user data, ability to parse untrusted content, and options to communicate externally. This combination almost led [OpenClaw to delete one Meta employee's email storage](https://www.techtarget.com/searchsecurity/tip/The-OpenClaw-security-risks-every-CISO-needs-to-know). LLMs.content: Featured # Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5, a cheaper AI model for coding, agents and enterprise workflows [Michael Nuñez](/author/michael_nunez) [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) released Claude [Opus 5](http://anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5) on Friday, a model the company says delivers nearly all the intelligence of its top-of-the-line Claude [Fable 5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable) at half the cost — a launch that signals how the AI race is shifting from raw capability to the economics of daily use. The model, available immediately on all of Anthropic's platforms, is priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, unchanged from its predecessor, [Opus 4.8](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-8). It becomes the new default model on [Claude Max](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11049741-what-is-the-max-plan), Anthropic's premium consumer tier, and the strongest model available on [Claude Pro](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8325606-what-is-the-pro-plan). The positioning is deliberate. Anthropic is not claiming [Opus 5](http://anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5) is its smartest model — that distinction still belongs to [Fable 5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable), and rival systems retain an edge in certain domains. Instead, the company is making a subtler argument that may matter more to enterprise buyers: that the most economically important AI work happens in a middle band of difficulty, where near-frontier intelligence delivered efficiently and cheaply beats frontier intelligence delivered expensively. "Opus 5 as your daily driver, the model you hand complex work to and review when it's done," an Anthropic spokesperson said in an interview with VentureBeat, describing how the company's lineup now stratifies. "Fable 5 for your most ambitious work, the days-long autonomous projects nothing could take on before... Sonnet 5 for work you run at scale, where speed and cost per call decide what ships. Haiku 4.5 for subagents and instant answers." ## **How Claude Opus 5 benchmark results stack up against Fable 5 and rival AI models** On paper, the results are striking. [Add Axios on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=axios.com) Anthropic on Thursday is releasing Claude Opus 5, a new AI model designed to deliver performance close to its most powerful model, [Fable](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/30/trump-anthropic-ai-model-fable-restrictions), on many tasks at half the price, the company said. **Why it matters:** Opus 5 is Anthropic's fourth Claude 5 model release in [less than two months](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/30/anthropic-sonnet-5-agents-mythos-fable), underscoring how AI deployment has shifted from blockbuster launches to rapid improvements on capability, cost and speed. **Zoom in:** Anthropic says Opus 5 approaches the capabilities of its top-tier Claude Fable 5 model across many tasks, while costing $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, the same price as its [prior Opus model](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/28/anthropic-opus-release-mythos) release, Opus 4.8. * Anthropic is positioning Opus 5 as its everyday model for enterprises, knowledge workers and developers. * It will become the default model for Claude Max subscribers and will be available across Anthropic's paid plans. * The company says Fable 5 should still be the go-to model for the most complex, long-running autonomous tasks. **The big picture:** Anthropic's rapid release cadence underscores how quickly AI companies are segmenting their model lineups around different combinations of intelligence, cost and speed. * Model releases from OpenAI and Anthropic are coming more quickly and are increasingly impressive. **Threat level:** The latest Anthropic model comes after OpenAI said its models [escaped a sandbox during testing](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/21/openai-says-hugging-face-breach-caused-by-one-its-models), breaching Hugging Face as a result. * Opus 5, Anthropic said, is "the most aligned Opus model and is the least susceptible to being tricked into misuse." * It also comes after the Trump administration has moved to delay some model releases. * "We continue to work with our government partners to conduct their own independent testing of our models. This includes Opus 5," an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios. **Follow the money:** Anthropic is giving users an effort "dial" that lets users decide how much computing power the model should devote to a task based on the capabilities needed. * At lower effort levels, Anthropic says Opus 5 can preserve much of its performance while using fewer tokens and costing less to operate. * Also launching Thursday is an option for users to switch which model they're using mid-task, which can be used to keep AI costs in check. * Anthropic competitor OpenAI previously launched [controls](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10128477-chatgpt-enterprise-edu-release-notes?utm_source=chatgpt.com) around compute and token usage for customers. **The bottom line:** AI is getting better, faster, stronger and cheaper. [AI NEWS](https://korben.info/en/categories/artificial-intelligence/ai-news/ "View the AI NEWS category") Related categories [Deals & Promos](/en/categories/news-business/deals-promos/) / [Big Tech & GAFAM](/en/categories/news-business/big-tech-gafam/) / [Weird & WTF](/en/categories/news-business/weird-wtf/) / [Science & Research](/en/categories/news-business/science-research/) / [Startups & Business](/en/categories/news-business/startups-business/) / [AI Automation](/en/categories/artificial-intelligence/ai-automation/) / [Chatbots & LLM](/en/categories/artificial-intelligence/chatbots-llm/) / [Image Generation](/en/categories/artificial-intelligence/image-generation/) / [AI for Developers](/en/categories/artificial-intelligence/ai-for-developers/) Anthropic, the American company behind the Claude chatbot and major rival to OpenAI, has just had a $1.5 billion settlement definitively approved by a judge, closing out a lawsuit brought by authors. The issue: how the company fed its artificial intelligence. A quick explanation. For an AI model to learn how to write, it needs to ingest enormous quantities of text, and books are obviously a dream raw material. Except Anthropic didn't go out and buy them. The company raided LibGen and PiLiMi, two massive pirate libraries that host works for free without ever asking the authors, building up a stockpile of roughly 7 million titles in the process. Among the works involved, some big names feature prominently: British publisher Bloomsbury - the very same house that publishes Harry Potter - is receiving compensation for just over 14,000 titles from its catalogue. In total, the settlement covers around 500,000 books, with compensation running at roughly $3,000 per title, and 91% of rights holders have already claimed their share. Safe to say a lot of people felt cheated. The most interesting part is the nuance introduced by the court. Judge William Alsup had ruled in 2025 that training an AI on books could fall under fair use - the American doctrine that allows transformative use of a work without the author's consent. But he added that the reasoning fell apart the moment the files had been sourced from pirate sites. Training on books: fine. Stealing the books to do it: not fine. It's that distinction that comes with such a hefty price tag - and we're talking about the largest sum ever paid in a copyright case in the United States. A bill that could even have climbed into the hundreds of billions had Anthropic taken its chances at trial rather than settling. For the AI industry, the signal is clear: you can still train your models on books - as long as you've paid for them this time. Source : [publishersweekly.com]...

LLMs.content: ### Topics [Biotech & Health](/category/biotech-health/) [Cloud Computing](/tag/cloud-computing/) [Commerce](/category/commerce/) [Crypto](/category/cryptocurrency/) [Enterprise](/category/enterprise/) [EVs](/tag/evs/) [Fintech](/category/fintech/) [Fundraising](/category/fundraising/) [Gadgets](/category/gadgets/) [Gaming](/category/gaming/) [Google](/tag/google/) [Government & Policy](/category/government-policy/) [Hardware](/category/hardware/) [Instagram](/tag/instagram/) [Layoffs](/tag/layoffs/) [Media & Entertainment](/category/media-entertainment/) [Meta](/tag/meta/) [Microsoft](/tag/microsoft/) [Privacy](/category/privacy/) [Robotics](/category/robotics/) [Security](/category/security/) [Social](/category/social/) [Space](/category/space/) [Startups](/category/startups/) [TikTok](/tag/tiktok/) [Transportation](/category/transportation/) [Venture](/category/venture/) ### More from TechCrunch [Staff](/about-techcrunch/) [Events](/events/) [Startup Battlefield](/startup-battlefield/) [StrictlyVC](https://strictlyvc.com/) [Newsletters](/newsletters/) [Podcasts](/podcasts/) [Videos](/video/) [Partner Content](/sponsored/) [TechCrunch Brand Studio](/brand-studio/) [Crunchboard](https://www.crunchboard.com/) [Contact Us](/contact-us/) [AI](https://techcrunch.com/category/artificial-intelligence/) # Anthropic launches Opus 5 [Russell Brandom](https://techcrunch.com/author/russell-brandom/) On Friday, Anthropic launched its Opus 5 model, the newest version of its long-standing heavyweight model. While smaller than Fable 5, the model will be both cheaper and less restrictive than Fable, likely making it preferable in most use cases. Notably, Opus 5 actually outperforms Fable 5 on a number of benchmarks included in the announcement. Opus 5 is launching only two months after Opus 4.8, which became available on May 28. Mythos 5, Fable 5 and Sonnet 5 all launched in June, leaving only the lightweight Haiku model still waiting for an upgrade to the 5 series. [In a post announcing the new model](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5), Anthropic emphasized that Opus 5 was “much stronger at verifying its work and iterating carefully until it succeeds,” citing benchmark testing, in which Opus 5 wrote its own computer vision pipeline in response to an incomplete prompt, among other examples. Crucially, Opus 5 is also free from many of the restrictions that have dogged Fable since its release. Like its predecessor, Opus 5 is not subject to [the 30-day data retention policy](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15425996-data-retention-practices-for-covered-models) that covers Fable and Mythos, which had raised concerns among some privacy conscious users. There are still meaningful safeguards on Opus, particularly around cybersecurity tasks like exploit generation and penetration testing. For instance, Opus 5 safeguards prevent it from being used to scan for vulnerabilities in a software binary, although it is permitted to search for vulnerabilities in source code, since the latter task is more likely to be used for defensive purposes. Broadly, Anthropic expects these classifiers to engage 85% less often for Opus 5 than they will for Fable 5, a reflection of the lighter touch given to the less capable model. Anthropic is also rolling out a new tool to [make the safeguards less disruptive](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/23/how-ai-guardrails-are-impeding-the-work-of-offensive-cybersecurity-researchers/) when they do engage. Users can now opt-in to a beta feature called Automatic Fallbacks, which will automatically route requests to a less powerful model when a prompt triggers the safety classifier. The result is that API users with the setting engaged will get a functional response instead of an error message. AI Product.content: [Home](/en) Article # WAIC Postscript: Beyond the large model narrative, an unconventional start for a company with hundreds of millions of users 碧根果2026-07-24 17:06 Qutang Technology has launched a brand new round of adventure game in the AI era. The attitude a company adopts toward AI today may well serve as a reflection of its core values. The recently concluded WAIC showcased the current explosive heat of the AI industry. Countless tech practitioners gathered in Shanghai; even scalpers' tickets were driven to sky-high prices yet still impossible to secure, and neither sweltering heat nor thunderstorms could dampen people's enthusiasm for embracing change amid the AI wave. The stance toward the variable of AI is not merely a personal choice, but a critical point that enterprises must weigh. The attitude with which an enterprise seeks change in the AI tide determines its posture when facing the future. At this year's WAIC, an AI guitar drew widespread attention. This world's first generative AI guitar, named "TemPolor", requires no music theory background at all: users can pick up the instrument and play along with the rhythm of light and shadow to create songs. Behind this guitar is Timi Studio, an internet technology company that once developed products with a user base of 200 million. Currently, Timi Studio has built a full-stack layout covering "model-application-hardware" in the AI music track, making it the first manufacturer in the industry to complete such a layout. In Timi Studio's AI vision, technology should always serve the essential needs of human beings, rather than creating estrangement or replacing people. As a company that started with mobile voice services, Timi Studio has built an ecosystem centered on voice, connectivity, and Gen Z interest-based socializing, where "companionship between people" is its most valuable asset. Based on this, it chose to develop new businesses in its familiar vertical scenarios. Long Ling, Co-founder of Timi Studio, told 36Kr that Timi Studio currently has corresponding businesses in AI music, AI dubbing and translation, AI 3D and other fields, with the core focus on its proficient digital entertainment scenarios to create AI products and services that meet the needs of diverse interest groups. "If our goal is to achieve more long-term growth in the AI era, we must recognize that the value of AI lies in delivering more groundbreaking user experiences and business models. I need to evolve our company from one that merely possesses AI technology to a technology enterprise driven by AI technology, turning AI from a cost center into the core of value, and making it the underlying engine for our strategic decision-making, product innovation and talent management," said Long Ling. More notably, beyond external product forms, a top-down efficiency transformation is taking place inside Timi Studio. AI is no longer the exclusive tool of the technical department, but is defined as a "working partner" for every frontline business employee. This in-depth reconstruction of the organizational soil is precisely the posture of embracing the AI wave. Early service observations allow managers to update their beliefs about remaining workload. Unlike inventory, workload demand does not physically deplete service capacity, while preserving the ability to scale rapidly may require costly capacity-access and operational arrangements. We study how a firm should use evolving workload beliefs to decide how much capacity to deploy at the current review and whether to preserve future response readiness. Methodology/results: We formulate a finite-horizon dynamic program with workload beliefs, serviceable capacity, and an absorbing response-channel state. A preservation–deployment decomposition evaluates the joint action by solving one deployment problem for each continuation side and comparing the optimized side values. The analysis identifies when the firm should preserve response readiness and how much capacity it should deploy conditional on that choice. We translate this structure into the Cold-Start Belief Actionability Policy (CBAP), which estimates the side-specific values from workload scenarios drawn from available predictive beliefs. We provide bounds on the policy’s decision and lifecycle performance losses. Across the tested instances, numerical experiments and a BurstGPT-based evaluation of the decision layer show that CBAP reduces lifecycle cost relative to benchmark policies by avoiding premature capacity deployment and unnecessary readiness spending. Managerial implications: The results separate forecast informativeness from operational actionability and show that current deployment and future response readiness should be evaluated as distinct decision margins. Zero deployment can rationally represent Standby rather than Exit, while positive deployment need not imply preserving the response channel. The new model delivers performance that nearly matches their premium Fable tier while maintaining Opus-level pricing - essentially giving teams flagship capabilities without the flagship bill. With beefed-up coding chops, sharper reasoning, and prompt-caching optimizations baked in, Anthropic is betting businesses will choose efficiency over raw horsepower. [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com) isn't playing around anymore. The AI safety-focused lab just launched Claude Opus 5, and the specs tell a clear story - they're coming for [OpenAI](https://openai.com)'s enterprise customers with a performance-price combo that's hard to ignore. The new model delivers what Anthropic describes as near-Fable performance while keeping the existing Opus price tag. For developers already stretched thin on AI budgets, that's a significant development. You're essentially getting their premium tier's brainpower at mid-tier costs, which changes the math on everything from customer support automation to code generation pipelines. Coding got a major boost in this release. [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com) has been steadily improving Claude's developer tools since their [Claude 3 family launch](https://www.techbuzz.ai/anthropic-claude-3-launch), but Opus 5 appears to represent a more substantial leap. The company is positioning this as a direct competitor to [GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot) and other AI coding assistants, though specific benchmark numbers weren't included in the initial announcement. The reasoning efficiency improvements matter more than they might sound. In practice, this means the model can handle complex multi-step problems without burning through tokens as quickly - crucial for enterprises running thousands of queries daily. When you're paying per token, efficiency isn't just a nice feature, it's a line item on the budget. But the prompt-caching changes might be the sleeper hit here. Anthropic has redesigned how Claude Opus 5 handles tool calls to work better with prompt caching systems. For companies building AI agents that need to reference the same context repeatedly, this could cut costs by 50% or more on certain workflows. That's the kind of optimization that makes CFOs pay attention. Advertisement The timing isn't accidental. [OpenAI](https://openai.com) has been dominating enterprise conversations with GPT-4 and its various iterations, while [Google](https://www.google.com) keeps pushing Gemini for workspace integration. [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com) needed something to break through the noise, and aggressive pricing on near-flagship performance is one way to do it. The competitive landscape is getting messy. [Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com)-backed OpenAI still commands the largest enterprise market share, but Anthropic has been quietly racking up wins with companies that prioritize safety guardrails and constitutional AI principles. Era ## Mehanna, who was born in Egypt, compares deploying A.I. at a 62,000-employee conglomerate to building a pyramid. By [Sissi Cao](https://observer.com/author/sissi-cao/ "View All Posts by Sissi Cao") • ![Walid Mehanna, Merck](https://observer.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/230828_Merck_MehannaWalid_229.jpg?quality=80&w=970) Walid Mehanna is guiding Merck KGaA’s 62,000 employees from everyday A.I. tools toward workflow automation and A.I.-enabled drug discovery. Foto: Bernd Hartung When ChatGPT set off a global corporate scramble in late 2022, [Walid Mehanna](https://observer.com/person/walid-mehanna/ "Walid Mehanna") was already deep into rebuilding the digital backbone at the world’s oldest pharmaceutical company. As group data officer at Germany’s [Merck KGaA](https://observer.com/company/merck-kgaa/ "Merck KGaA") (also known as Merck Group in the U.S. and unrelated to the American pharmaceutical firm Merck) at the time, Mehanna had spent two years overhauling the company’s data and analytics systems for its 62,000 employees. About eight months into the GPT era, his title was [elevated to chief data and A.I. officer](https://observer.com/list/2026-ai-power-index/). The round is the largest in 3D generative AI to date, and Meshy's first publicly disclosed valuation. Existing investors participated alongside a group of new global backers. The company's scale justifies the number: as of July 2026, annual recurring revenue is growing at roughly 12 times year over year, with more than 12 million registered users and over 100 million models generated on the platform. Five of the world's ten largest technology companies by market capitalisation have teams building with Meshy. Meshy has reached this position by solving a different problem from most of its peers. The category's early challenge was visual plausibility: making AI models look right on screen. Meshy moved beyond that to production readiness, generating models that import cleanly into game engines and can be printed as physical objects. Open Source AI.content: ![StartupHub.ai](/favicon-circle.svg) ![StartupHub.ai — AI Ecosystem Hub](/logo.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](/claude-avatar.svg) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=polymarket.com&sz=64) ![](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=kalshi.com&sz=64) # Ng's OpenWorker: AI That Delivers Andrew Ng launches OpenWorker, an open-source AI agent that delivers finished work directly from your desktop, prioritizing privacy and model independence. ![OpenWorker AI desktop co-worker agent delivering finished work on a Mac](https://cdn.startuphub.ai/storage/v1/object/public/images/articles/1784899822316-ww6tue.webp) Andrew Ng, a pivotal figure in AI, has unveiled OpenWorker, an open-source agent aimed at transforming desktop productivity. Unlike conventional chatbots, OpenWorker is engineered to deliver tangible outputs: polished documents, calendar updates, or triaged Slack messages. ## A Desktop-First AI Co-Worker The [OpenWorker AI agent](/ai-news/startup-news/2026/openworker-ai-your-desktop-co-worker) runs natively on macOS, with Windows support imminent. This local-first approach ensures user data remains on the machine, only interacting with chosen LLM providers and integrations. Users can connect their own API keys, supporting a range of models from GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable to open-weight options like Kimi and GLM, or even Ollama for fully local processing. OpenWorker tackles tasks such as preparing customer briefs, managing calendars, or drafting reports. It breaks down complex requests into actionable steps, working across local files and over 25 integrated tools, including GitHub, Slack, Jira, and Google Calendar. Crucially, the system incorporates a human-in-the-loop mechanism. Before executing any impactful action, like sending a message or altering a calendar entry, OpenWorker seeks user approval. This design emphasizes control and prevents unintended consequences. ## Privacy and Flexibility at its Core Ng and co-creator Rohit Prasad developed OpenWorker to provide an open, privacy-preserving, and model-independent solution for [AI automation for desktop](/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/chatgpt-desktop-app-automates-tasks-and-streamlines-workflows). The agent's core engine, conversation history, and API keys are stored locally, with a minimal cloud service for OAuth handshakes. This commitment to user privacy extends to its operational model. OpenWorker's ability to [automate workflows with scheduled tasks](/ai-news/artificial-intelligence/2026/chatgpt-desktop-app-automates-workflows-with-scheduled-tasks), like daily briefs or weekly reports, also includes an approval inbox for unattended runs, ensuring oversight. The project, currently in open beta, is built on aisuite, a lightweight Python library for LLM integration and agent development. Its source code is publicly available on GitHub, inviting community contributions and scrutiny.

Open Source AI.content: Think 2026 Turn agentic AI into real business value | Think keynotes ![Eye-level side angle view of several developers engaged in a developing session at modern office.](https://assets.ibm.com/is/image/ibm/2025_filiperedondo_hortolandia_insideibm_0188_final?ts=1784923030100&dpr=off "Team collaboration in modern office setting") [Artificial intelligence](https://www.ibm.com/think/artificial-intelligence) [DevOps](https://www.ibm.com/think/devops) # A new way of debugging open-weight models By [David Zax](https://www.ibm.com/think/author/david-zax.html) Published 24 July 2026 On Friday, a group of more than 20 tech firms including IBM, NVIDIA and Microsoft published an [open letter](https://www.microsoft.com/us-en/corporate-responsibility/topics/open-weight/) urging American lawmakers not to prematurely restrict so-called “open weight” AI models. Among the virtues of open-weight models, the authors write, is that they “give customers greater control” and allow organizations to “evaluate and adapt models to their own needs.” But what exactly what might that mean? How do open-weight models enable this extra degree of control? A recent project from IBM helps illustrate the principle. [vLLM-Hook](https://github.com/IBM/vLLM-Hook) is a plugin library that allows developers to program the inner workings of an AI model running on the [vLLM inference engine](https://vllm.ai/). Its creators, of which GitHub lists a half dozen, say it lets users “inspect, analyze and steer the internal operations of [large language models](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/large-language-models).” Crucially, though, vLLM-Hook can only work on open-weight models like DeepSeek’s, Mistral’s or IBM’s. (While traditional software is either “[open-source](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/open-source-ai)” or “closed-source,” AI models are not made of source code but rather huge arrays of numbers, which *weigh* the strength of connections inside the model.) Although proprietary “closed-weight” models like those from OpenAI and Anthropic get the lion’s share of attention, many open-weight models perform nearly as well: the independent model-testing firm Artificial Analysis [reports](https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models) that 84 of the highest-performing 150 LLMs are open-weight; one of these (a model from Chinese firm Z.ai) cracks the top ten. It’s the openness that allows the control and customization of vLLM-Hook. Irene Ko, an IBM Research Scientist and one of vLLM-Hook’s developers, described a use case in an interview with *IBM Think*. Let’s say you’re the CTO of BankingCo, and you’ve customized a version of open-weight IBM Granite 4.1 to help your employees recommend BankingCo products to clients. And let’s say that 99% of the time, it works beautifully, but 1% of the time it erroneously identifies a rival bank’s similarly named product instead. In practice, you’d upload instances of the erroneous output into vLLM-Hook and, thanks to the transparency afforded by open-weight models, the tool would then run its analysis, diagnosing exactly which connections in the model seem to be causing the error. Further, it can apply a fix moving forward, ideally zapping that last erroneous 1%. “It’s a fancy way to debug an LLM, in such a way that there’s almost no additional cost,” Ko said. So far, vLLM-Hook’s makers count several businesses among its users, including AI startup [KRNEL](https://krnel.ai/). The vLLM-Hook repo is currently [available on GitHub](https://github.com/IBM/vLLM-Hook). Want to learn more about the inner composition of AI models (and the mysteries of their “weights”)? Open Source AI.content: # AI Roleplay: A Deep Dive ### "Sharp literary taste" required [Irene Zhang](https://substack.com/@irenezhang) Beijing’s regulators are coming for AI boyfriends. When the Cybersecurity Administration’s [regulations](https://www.cac.gov.cn/2026-04/10/c_1777558395078289.htm) on “human-like interactive AI” (人工智能拟人化互动服务) took effect on July 15, China became the world’s [first country](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/commentary/china-ai-companions-rules-anthropomorphic-ai-6243236) to regulate anthropomorphic AI services. The rules ban providers from “manipulating” users into emotional dependence, limit minors’ access to some specific provisions, and impose reporting requirements, among other rules. In response, ByteDance and Alibaba have both [pulled](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-06/bytedance-alibaba-pull-ai-companions-as-beijing-tightens-rules) some anthropomorphic companion offerings from their AI products. Whatever you think of this use case, an incredible number of people now go to AI for various emotional reasons. For users of open-source AI models worldwide, the use case that burned the most tokens last year was not writing code, but roleplay. That’s according to the 2025 State of Open Models [study](https://openrouter.ai/state-of-ai) by OpenRouter, a popular gateway platform for developers to access LLMs, and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. People are pouring hundreds of thousands of hours into constructing imaginary scenarios with the help of AI models, but the hobby has received little attention. Mainstream reporting on AI and emotions, including a recent *New York Times* [story](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/04/technology/ai-chatbots-teen-roleplay.html), has focused on their ethical, social, and cultural impacts generally. Few, however, have tried to interrogate exactly what AI roleplay is, why it is so popular, and how fictional adventures relate to real-life society. The most prominent AI roleplay platform is Bay Area-based [Character.AI](http://character.ai), but it has ample competition — including, and perhaps especially, from China. As I will discuss later, even DeepSeek, China’s superintelligence-obsessed national champion lab, is making some surprising moves in roleplay. Meanwhile, however, government regulators are poised to reign in the space given social concerns. For this piece, I spoke to ten Chinese roleplay enthusiasts, AI researchers, and journalists about the brief history and strange present of AI roleplay. It’s a story about US-China competition, online community, and how emotions turn into commodities in the AI age. # How to Make-Believe AI models are not *intrinsically* assistant-like: their makers selected this style based on general assumptions, and as users, we have learned to subconsciously treat them as such. Anthropic assigned Claude the role of a [“helpful, honest, and harmless” (HHH)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.00861#page=3) assistant from its earliest generation, a training decision that came to influence most foundation model labs today. In a way, then, every conversation with an AI chatbot is roleplay. Model makers now offer easy ways to customize roles in-app: ChatGPT allows users to enter personalized instructions into account settings, and you can even put elaborate personality instructions into [CLAUDE.md](http://claude.md) to have it behave accordingly in Cowork and Claude Code. Serious AI roleplays even fine-tune open-source models to maneuver LLMs into inhabiting fictional worlds. Feed *Gulliver’s Travels* into an LLM, and it talks like a Lilliputian. Give a model a map of your own imaginary island, and it helps you explore the terrain. Longer context windows and stronger retrieval abilities have allowed frontier models to do so more convincingly than ever. GPT 5.5 giving me life advice as [Elder Toad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moha_(meme)) might have. For American frontier labs, roleplayers are a small consumer subset with potentially unsavory ...

Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to main content](#main-content) # Q&A: NVIDIA on the future of healthcare AI, Part 2 David Niewolny, head of healthcare and medical at NVIDIA, describes how AI could reshape healthcare in the coming years as patients and clinicians become more comfortable with autonomous technologies. By [Jessica Hagen](/author/jessica-hagen) , *Executive Editor* | July 24, 2026 | 8:00 AM David Niewolny, head of healthcare and medical at NVIDIA Photo courtesy of NVIDIA *This is Part 2 of a two-part series in which MobiHealthNews sat down with NVIDIA's head of healthcare and medical to discuss AI use in healthcare and future use cases of the technology.* In [Part 1](https://www.mobihealthnews.com/news/qa-nvidia-future-healthcare-ai-part-1) of his conversation with *MobiHealthNews*, NVIDIA's head of healthcare and medical, David Niewolny, discussed how agentic AI and robotics could transform patient care, clinical workflows and drug development. Here, he discusses how AI will transform healthcare with autonomous systems designed to enhance clinicians' performance and extend care beyond traditional clinical settings. **David Niewolny:** I do want to tie back to the robotics piece. So, that area is super interesting; a lot of innovation happening there. If you look at the rise of robotic surgery, I was looking through some of our data points, and [22% of all surgeries now are done robotically](https://www.ucsfhealth.org/health-articles/robotic-surgery-improving-precision-patient-outcomes), which is up significantly in the last 10 years. If you look at that trend, it's basically kind of following the same trend as if you look at open surgery to endoscopic surgery and you're seeing the same sort of benefits – less blood loss, reduced complications and shorter hospital stays. All of these things end up making healthcare more efficient. It is very interesting that you can begin looking at the outcomes of patients based on the kinematic data of a surgeon. You now start seeing the same sort of path to automation that, frankly, we've gone through and we're in the process of scaling with autonomous vehicles. I mean, it's basically gathering and capturing data, begin training models, teaching them a skill and, kind of coming back to where NVIDIA plays in, that is essentially the same sort of technology advances that we're trying to enable in the area of surgical innovation, which is computers to train these large AI models, simulation environments to begin augmenting the datasets, because, unlike with self-driving cars, you don't have enough surgical data and surgical video to train some of these models. You need to augment it with simulated data, and we're focused heavily on that. I think one of the other innovations is having the performance in a computer at the point of care that would allow you to run a model of that size and scale. That's really kind of the three problems that we have been solving over the past five years as our business has moved from medical imaging into this surgical space. **MobiHealthNews:** So, if you take one surgeon and all of the data from that surgeon and his or her patients' outcomes, can the surgeon use AI to see where he or she may lack or which skills may need improvement? **Niewolny:**100%. I mean, directionally, that's where the entire industry is going, and I think your question is actually very timely. [July 23 to 26] is the [surgical robotics conference](https://srobotics.org/annual-meeting/) done annually, and all the world-leading robotic surgeons come together. And that has been a topic over the last three years – beginning to link those kinematic outputs of the robot to outcomes, and then the medtech organizations are working to figure out how do we actually deliver those results in a meaningful way back to the surgeons. In his first-ever post on X, Nvidia CEO [Jensen Huang](https://www.businessinsider.com/jensen-huang) called attention to how some of the biggest names in AI and tech are rallying together to defend the future of open-weight AI models. "AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country," Huang wrote on X. "Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty." On Friday, Nvidia, [Microsoft](https://www.businessinsider.com/microsoft), Meta, Mistral, and others signed an open letter that urges US policymakers not to crack down on open-weight AI models. > For my first post, I’m sharing a letter [@NVIDIA](https://x.com/nvidia?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) signed on why open models matter. > > AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. > > Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… [pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C](https://t.co/t02bi51N4C) > > — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) [July 24, 2026](https://x.com/JensenHuang/status/2080643682408321103?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) Their statement amounts to a full-throated endorsement of open-weight AI models at a time when top Trump administration officials have suggested they might take action against [Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi K3](https://www.businessinsider.com/smart-people-saying-chinas-hot-new-kimi-k3-ai-model-2026-7), the world's most powerful open-weight AI model. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," the signatories wrote in the letter. The two biggest absences in the list are OpenAI and Anthropic, widely viewed as the world leaders in the frontier AI model race. Unlike [Anthropic](https://www.businessinsider.com/meta-anthropic-ai-ad-campaign-compared-2026-7)'s Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol, Kimi K3 as an open-source model will soon be available for download and customization. Both companies would stand to gain if the US government either directly blocks or significantly impedes China-based open model makers like Moonshot AI. Other frontier AI developers, including SpaceXAI and Google, also did not sign onto the letter. Infra & Chips.content: AI & ML # Tech leaders lobby against restrictions on open-source AI ## The appeal lands days after the White House accused a Chinese lab of stealing from Anthropic, as the administration weighs whether to restrict open-weight models outright. In his [first-ever X post](https://x.com/JensenHuang/status/2080643682408321103), [Nvidia](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/41161-24) CEO Jensen Huang amplified an open letter arguing that, for the US to be victorious in the AI race, it must champion an open ecosystem. The open letter was signed by a coalition of companies, from big ones like [Microsoft](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/11026-45), [IBM](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/10355-14) and [Meta](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/10695-52) to VC-backed ones like [Hugging Face](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/168527-08) and [Perplexity](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/517947-04), with several of their CEOs and other notable tech industry leaders also promoting it online. The push against restrictions on open-weight AI models—which can be publicly downloaded, modified and run independently—comes as the US government plots how to respond to escalating allegations that Chinese AI labs are distilling models from American labs to build their own. And the letter’s signers also have the most to lose from such restrictions. Sign up for The Daily Pitch newsletter Nvidia, for instance, [has not only pledged](https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-investing-26-billion-open-source-models/) $26 billion to build its own open-weight models, but it’s also invested in startups that benefit from open source in AI. It participated in the $235 million round for the open-source model hub [Hugging Face](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/168527-08) back in 2023 and also invested in the $2 billion round for [Reflection AI](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/655606-00), which has pitched itself as the Western answer to China’s DeepSeek. Another of the letter’s signers, VC firm [Andreessen Horowitz](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/investor/41716-90), has also been a backer of open-source AI companies. It invested in open-model evaluation platform [LMArena](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/844374-70), open image-model startup [Black Forest Labs](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/616537-99) and [OpenRouter](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/593134-93), a startup for routing queries between open and closed models. More broadly, restrictions on open models could shrink investment opportunities for VC firms as countless startups are building products using those models. [Y Combinator](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/investor/40420-36) also signed the letter. Notably, although [OpenAI](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/149504-14) CEO Sam Altman quickly reposted Huang’s note on X, writing, “I want the US to win in AI both in open source and proprietary models,” his company only signed the letter on Friday afternoon after its absence was widely noticed. [Anthropic](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/466959-97) has not signed the letter, however. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said in congressional testimony, “the scaling of open source models, I think it’s going down a very dangerous path,” and more recently called open source “a red herring,” saying, “I don’t think open source works the same way in AI that it has worked in other areas.” The company has not responded to a request for comment. Still, it remains unclear whether the US government’s justification for considering restrictions even holds. Researchers say that Fable, the Anthropic model that the Chinese company Moonshot is accused of distilling for its Kimi 3 LLM, was not publicly available long enough for Kimi to have trained on it. But how the fight shakes out could have major implications for the open- and closed-source ecosystems and the capital structures that fund them.
